Females of the Umbrella squid reach a mantle length of 23.0 centimeters [Li = 23.0 centimeters] at death, a size that is notably larger than the 19.8 centimeters [Li = 19.8 centimeters] recorded for males. This sexual size dimorphism is a common feature among histioteuthids and likely reflects the considerable energetic demands placed on females for egg production. Field studies have documented that females attain a mantle length of 11.0 centimeters [Lp = 11.0 centimeters] at the onset of sexual maturation, whereas males begin their pubertal development at a much smaller body size, approximately 5.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5.5 centimeters]. This divergence in size at maturity between the sexes is consistent with a life-history strategy in which males prioritize early reproductive opportunity while females defer reproduction until they have accumulated sufficient reserves to support a large energy investment.

The reproductive output of this species, measured as the cumulative number of eggs produced over a female's lifetime at death, has been estimated at 275,000 eggs per individual (275000)  in specimens maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This figure is remarkably high for a mid-sized oceanic squid and underscores the strong selection for fecundity in an environment where early-life mortality rates are presumably very high. The enormous oocyte count is coupled with a very small initial investment per offspring; the wet weight of each newly hatched paralarva is a mere 0.000024 grams [Wwb = 0.000024 grams]. These tiny paralarvae emerge from eggs that measure approximately 0.5 millimeters in the longest dimension and 0.3 millimeters in width.

In comparison to many coastal squid species that experience rapid juvenile growth and die within a single year, the Umbrella squid exhibits a relatively protracted life history when maintained at the cool temperatures of its preferred mesopelagic habitat. The maximum lifespan recorded for captive females kept at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] is 450 days [am = 450 days], a duration that allows for an extended period of somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive activity. This female lifespan of 450 days [am = 450 days] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] is notably longer than that reported for smaller, epipelagic squid species that often complete their entire life cycle in under six months. The extended lifespan permits females to achieve the larger body sizes necessary to accommodate the large cumulative fecundity of 275,000 eggs (275000)  recorded under these same thermal conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].

The size at which females initiate puberty, measured as a mantle length of 11.0 centimeters [Lp = 11.0 centimeters], represents a nearly twofold increase over the initial mantle length recorded at death for males of 19.8 centimeters [Li = 19.8 centimeters] — though it is important to note that female size at death is also larger. This suggests that females allocate a substantial proportion of their early growth to building a robust somatic framework before shifting resources toward gametogenesis. The male puberty size of 5.5 centimeters [Lp = 5.5 centimeters] is barely a quarter of the maximum female size, indicating that males mature early in life. The differential in size at puberty between the sexes — 11.0 centimeters [Lp = 11.0 centimeters] in females versus 5.5 centimeters in males — is among the most extreme documented for any member of the family Histioteuthidae.

The very small initial body mass of 0.000024 grams [Wwb = 0.000024 grams] at hatching implies that a newly hatched paralarva relies on a rapid transition to planktonic feeding success; even a short delay in first prey capture would be physiologically catastrophic for an organism of this minuscule starting size. Females must effectively double their mantle length from the 11.0 centimeters [Lp = 11.0 centimeters] at puberty to the 23.0 centimeters [Li = 23.0 centimeters] recorded at death, a significant growth increment that likely requires sustained access to a productive prey field of crustaceans and small fish throughout their adult life. Given a lifespan of 450 days [am = 450 days] at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females appear to grow continuously but at a decelerating rate, investing heavily in the production of numerous small eggs rather than a smaller number of larger offspring.
